name: RecMem

paper.title: RecMem: Recurrence-based Memory Consolidation for Efficient and Effective Long-Running LLM Agents

construction.unit: interaction unit: one user-assistant exchange (in LoCoMo, two consecutive messages) with its timestamp
construction.kept_as: verbatim turn until a topic recurs; then LLM-written episodes and extracted facts
construction.processing: embed every turn (no LLM); an LLM writes episodes and facts only when enough similar turns have piled up, or when a turn merges into an existing episode

organization.structure: three flat vector stores: subconscious turns, episodes, semantic facts
organization.stores: subconscious (raw turns), episodic (narratives), semantic (atomic facts); one collection per conversation

management.operations: promote a recurring cluster into 1-3 episodes plus refined facts; merge a new turn into its nearest episode by LLM rewrite
management.conflicts: the fact refiner is told to drop facts already known and to record changes as time-anchored updates; answer prompt prefers the most recent memory
management.forgetting: turns that are consolidated are deleted from the subconscious store (code only; the paper says they stay)

retrieval.candidates: dense top-k from each of the three stores
retrieval.selection: fixed per-store top-k by cosine; no reranker, no threshold (semantic threshold 0)
retrieval.budget: k_sub = 10 turns, k_epi = 5 episodes, k_sem = 10 facts

use.context: episodes, raw turns and facts as three bulleted lists in one prompt, each sorted by similarity
use.reasoning: single answer call; the LoCoMo prompt caps the answer at 5-6 words

classify.note: Tiers because turns are promoted from the subconscious store to episodes and facts; within each tier storage is flat.

stages.ingestion: Each user-assistant exchange becomes one unit, prefixed with its (session) timestamp and embedded with text-embedding-3-small; no LLM is called at this point.
stages.construction: A turn that finds enough similar turns in the subconscious store (cosine above θsim, count reaching θcount) triggers an LLM that writes 1-3 time-ordered episodes from the cluster; semantic refinement then extracts under 10 new facts that the episode left out.
stages.organization: Three flat vector stores per conversation: unconsolidated raw turns, episode narratives and atomic facts.
stages.update: Before gating, a turn is compared with its nearest episode; above the threshold an LLM decides whether it continues that topic and rewrites the episode, followed by fact refinement on that turn. In the code, consolidated or merged turns are removed from (or never enter) the subconscious store.
stages.retrieval: The question embedding pulls 10 raw turns, 5 episodes and 10 facts by cosine similarity.
stages.answer: One LLM call reads the three lists (episodes, raw turns, facts) under a prompt that explains their roles and asks to avoid double counting.

summary: Defers LLM consolidation: turns sit as embedded raw text until a topic recurs enough times, then an LLM writes episodes and refines facts, cutting memory-building tokens by up to 87% versus Mem0 and A-Mem.
notes:
Venue: ACL 2026 Findings, verified on ACL Anthology (2026.findings-acl.1619); the arXiv comment and repo README say the same. Text from arXiv v1 PDF (pdftotext). Code read at commit a84252f6 (2026-05-15, the only commit, 'Initial open-source release').
DESIGN: §3.2-3.6, §4.1, App. B, C, E; code rec_mem.py. control.construction = fixed-rule because whether and when to consolidate is a similarity/count rule (the content is then written by a prompted LLM); control.management = prompted-llm for the should_merge decision. fidelity = mixed: unconsolidated turns are verbatim, episodes are rewritten, facts extracted. Paper vs code: the code deletes consolidated turns from the subconscious store, although the Limitations section says every unit stays retrievable (see mechanism.paper_vs_code).

sources.code_note: The repository has a single commit (2026-05-15, the arXiv date), released as the paper's code. The README gives the exact LoCoMo and LongMemEval-S commands; their flags are used here where the Python defaults differ (e.g. min_consolidation_cnt default 6, merge threshold default 0.75).

abstract.text: RecMem argues that memory systems waste tokens by running an LLM over every incoming turn. It keeps each exchange as an embedded raw record in a cheap 'subconscious' store and calls the LLM only when a topic recurs: once enough similar turns accumulate, they are turned into episode narratives, and a refinement step extracts the specific facts the narrative dropped. At question time it reads a fixed number of raw turns, episodes and facts by embedding similarity. On LoCoMo and LongMemEval-S the authors report higher accuracy than Mem0, A-Mem and MemoryOS with far fewer memory-building tokens.
abstract.note: Summary in our words; the original abstract is on arXiv.

headline: No LLM runs on a turn until its topic has come up about five times (θcount 5, θsim 0.7 on LoCoMo); until then the turn is only embedded.
The answer model reads 10 raw turns next to 5 episodes and 10 facts; removing the raw-turn store costs the most (81.10 to 51.88 on LoCoMo).
In the released code, turns that get consolidated are deleted from the raw store, so only never-consolidated turns remain verbatim.

paper_vs_code.topic: Do consolidated turns stay in the raw store?
paper_vs_code.paper: Limitations: every unit is kept verbatim and stays retrievable whether or not it was consolidated
paper_vs_code.code: clustered turns are deleted after consolidation; the triggering turn and merged turns never enter the raw store

paper_vs_code.paper: |R_i| ≥ θcount, where R_i are past turns only (Eq. 5)
paper_vs_code.code: past hits + 1 for the new turn ≥ θcount, so 4 similar past turns suffice at θcount 5 (App. B's example matches the code)

paper_vs_code.paper: in-place LLM merge whenever similarity to the nearest episode ≥ θsim (Eq. 6)
paper_vs_code.code: separate merge threshold (README sets it equal to θsim); the LLM may answer should_merge = no, and the turn then goes to the recurrence gate

open_questions: Because consolidated turns are deleted, the 'no subconscious' ablation (51.88) removes only never-consolidated turns; the paper does not report how many turns that is, so it is unclear how much evidence exists only in raw form.
On LoCoMo each baseline keeps its own answer prompt (App. E.3) while RecMem's prompt explains its three memory types, so accuracy gaps mix memory design and prompting.
The ablation keeps each module's budget fixed rather than total context fixed, so removing a store also shrinks the context.

glance.a: Three kinds: a raw exchange with its timestamp, an LLM-written episode narrative, and a one-sentence fact.

glance.q: When is the LLM called while building memory?
glance.a: Only when a turn is close to an existing episode (merge) or when about five similar turns have accumulated (consolidation). Other turns are just embedded.
Recurring topics are rewritten into 3-6 sentence episodes and extracted facts; the raw turns of those topics are then deleted in the code.
No. Each store returns its top-k by cosine similarity to the question.

glance.q: What does the answer model read?
glance.a: 5 episodes, 10 raw turns and 10 facts in one prompt.

key_numbers.label: Consolidate when
key_numbers.value: ≥ 5 similar turns (sim > 0.7) on LoCoMo · ≥ 4 (sim > 0.6) on LongMemEval-S

components.role: Embeds turns, episodes, facts and questions
Writes and merges episodes, refines facts

discussion.takeaway: An LLM does not need to process every turn: consolidating only recurring topics, while keeping the rest as embedded raw text, keeps accuracy at or above the tested memory systems at a fraction of their memory-building tokens.

claims.claim: Eager per-turn consolidation is the main cost driver of current memory systems.
claims.evidence: Construction tokens per LoCoMo conversation: Mem0 1520.8K, A-Mem 1459.9K vs RecMem 193.2K (-87.3%, -86.8%), GPT-4.1-mini. Table 1, §4.2

claims.claim: Cheaper construction does not cost accuracy.
claims.evidence: Best overall among memory systems: LoCoMo 81.10 vs A-Mem 68.83; LongMemEval-S 76.80, best of all methods including full context (66.20). Tables 1-2
LongMemEval-S temporal 68.42 vs 62.41 for Mem0 (GPT-4.1-mini). Table 2, §4.2

claims.claim: All three stores contribute; the raw store most.
claims.evidence: 81.10 full; 79.94 without episodes; 70.58 without facts; 51.88 without raw turns. Fig. 2, §4.3
Direct extraction without episode reference 74.22 vs 79.94 for the refinement variant, both without episodic retrieval. Fig. 2, §4.3

limits: θsim and θcount are set by hand per dataset and may need recalibration for other interaction densities.
Recurrence is a proxy for importance; one-off but critical details get no episode or fact and rely on the raw store.
Evaluated only offline on public benchmarks.
reading: In the released code, turns that were consolidated or merged are removed from the raw store, so the Limitations claim that every turn stays retrievable does not hold for the code; for recurring topics the answer model sees only LLM text.
Full context still beats RecMem on LoCoMo (84.18 vs 81.10 with GPT-4.1-mini; 76.43 vs 72.47 with GPT-4o-mini); the lead over all methods is on LongMemEval-S only.
Thresholds differ per dataset (0.7/5 vs 0.6/4); the sensitivity sweeps that show a peak at the LoCoMo defaults are run on the LoCoMo test questions themselves (App. C).

On LoCoMo each baseline answers with its own prompt, while on LongMemEval-S all use RecMem's prompt body (App. E.3); RecMem's A-Mem LoCoMo score is 68.83 in Table 1 but 69.7 in Table 3, and full context 84.18 vs 84.8.
Construction savings come partly from the merge path: every turn close to an existing episode still triggers an LLM merge and a fact refinement, so the cost depends on how often topics repeat.
